blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

A sliding window is a **contiguous range** `[left, right]` of an array or string that you grow on the right and shrink on the left, while keeping a running summary (a sum, a count map, a set) up to date. Because both ends only move forward, the whole scan is **O(n)**, instead of examining every subarray in O(n²).

| Window type | Rule | Typical problems |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed size** k | Add the new element, remove the one that left | Permutation in String, Sliding Window Maximum, max sum of k elements |
| **Variable, longest** | Grow while the window is valid; shrink only when it becomes invalid | Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Longest Repeating Character Replacement |
| **Variable, shortest** | Grow until valid; then shrink as far as it stays valid, recording each time | Minimum Window Substring, smallest subarray with sum >= target |
"subarray" or "substring" (contiguous), "longest", "shortest", "at most k", "contains all of", "without repeating".
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text: The template is always the same: **expand** `right`, **update** the summary, **while the window breaks the rule, shrink** `left`, then **record** the answer. What changes is the rule and the summary.
Use `int[26]` or `int[128]` for letter counts, a `HashMap` for general keys, and an `ArrayDeque` of indices when you need the maximum or minimum of the window.

blocks.title: SlidingWindow.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** `characterReplacement` never shrinks `maxFreq` when a letter leaves. That is deliberate: a stale (too large) `maxFreq` can only make the window look *more* valid, and the window only matters when it beats the best length seen, which requires a genuinely larger `maxFreq`. Know this trick, and be ready to explain it.

- **Shrinking too early or too late.** Longest-window problems shrink only when invalid; shortest-window problems shrink while still valid.
- **Updating the answer in the wrong place.** Record it after the shrink loop for "longest", inside it for "shortest".
- **Negative numbers** break "sum >= target" windows, because shrinking no longer reduces the sum monotonically. Use prefix sums and a map or deque instead.
- **Counting with `HashMap<Character,Integer>`** in a hot loop is slower than `int[26]`; and `map.get(c) == map2.get(c)` compares `Integer` references.

Two pointers is the general idea of two indices moving through the data. A sliding window is the case where the two pointers delimit a contiguous range and you maintain a summary of what is inside it. Both are O(n) because each pointer only moves forward.
blocks.title: Interview angle: How is the sliding window different from two pointers?
Key points
blocks.text:
- A window `[left, right]` grows on the right and shrinks on the left, O(n) overall
- Fixed windows add one and remove one; variable windows shrink while the rule is broken
- Longest: record after shrinking; shortest: record while shrinking
- Use `int[26]` for letters and a deque of indices for window maximum
- Negative numbers break sum-based windows

blocks.title: Practise and track them
blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Sliding Window** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

items.question: Why is the sliding window solution O(n) although it has a `while` inside a `for`?
items.answer: `left` only moves forward and never past `right`, so across the whole run it moves at most n steps in total. Each element enters and leaves the window once.

items.question: What does the deque hold in Sliding Window Maximum, and why is it decreasing?
items.answer: Indices of candidates for the maximum, with decreasing values. A smaller element before a newer larger one can never be the maximum of any later window, so it is removed from the back; the front is the current maximum.

items.question: Why can't you use a sliding window to find the shortest subarray with sum at least k when the array has negative numbers?
items.answer: Adding an element no longer always increases the sum and removing one no longer always decreases it, so there is no monotone rule telling you which end to move.
